readerTitle: When feedback makes people worse at their jobs
caseNote: 실제 연구 (Kluger & DeNisi, 1996 피드백 메타분석) + 가상 사례 (B2B 컨설팅 회사, 청소 서비스 회사)
insight: 피드백은 주는 것만으로 효과가 나지 않는다. 사람이 아니라 행동과 그 결과를 가리켜야 고칠 수 있는 정보가 된다.
misconception: 피드백은 많이, 솔직하게 주기만 하면 성과가 오른다. 부드럽게 감싸서 주면 더 잘 받아들인다.

sources.text: Kluger, A. N., & DeNisi, A. (1996). The effects of feedback interventions on performance: A historical review, a meta-analysis, and a preliminary feedback intervention theory. Psychological Bulletin, 119(2), 254–284.
컨설팅 회사와 청소 회사 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Kluger & DeNisi(1996): 607개 효과크기 분석, 평균적으로는 피드백이 성과를 높였지만 1/3 이상의 경우 성과를 낮췄다는 결과. 카드에는 "more than a third"로 적었습니다. 게시 전 원문으로 다시 확인하세요.
같은 논문의 해석: 피드백이 주의를 과제에서 자기 자신(자존감, 자기 이미지)으로 옮길수록 효과가 약해진다는 '피드백 개입 이론'. 카드에는 단순화해서 "tended to help less"로 적었고, 인과를 단정하지 않았습니다.

cards.title: When feedback makes people worse at their jobs
body: Researchers reviewed hundreds of studies on feedback at work and in labs. On average, feedback helped.
But in more than a third of cases, people performed *worse* after getting it. Feedback was the problem, not the cure.

image.label: Manager giving notes as a worker's progress line dips
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 매니저가 메모지를 건네는 장면, 뒤쪽 벽에 걸린 성과 그래프 선이 위로 가다가 아래로 꺾임. 실제 회사 로고 없음.

cards.title: The client caught the mistake.
body: You run a small consulting firm. A junior analyst sent a client report with wrong numbers, for the second time this month. The client noticed.

options.text: Message today: "You need to be more careful with client work."
options.feedback: It's fast and honest, but it judges the person without saying what went wrong. They may feel attacked and still not know what to fix.

options.text: Save it for the quarterly review, between two pieces of praise
options.feedback: It feels kind, but the lesson arrives weeks late and the key point gets lost between compliments.

options.text: Talk today: name the wrong table, what it cost with the client, and one check to add before sending
options.feedback: The analyst gets something concrete to change, while the mistake is still fresh. It takes more effort to prepare.

cards.title: Feedback can backfire.
body: In 1996, Avraham Kluger and Angelo DeNisi combined results from 607 measured effects of feedback. Overall, feedback raised performance. Yet **more than a third** of the effects were negative.
One pattern stood out. Feedback that pulled attention toward the person, their worth or self-image, tended to help less. Feedback that kept attention on the task tended to help more.

cards.title: Feedback points at behavior, not the person.
body: **Good feedback** is information about a specific action, what it caused, and what to do next. It describes something the person can see and change.
"You're careless" is a verdict on the person. "The revenue table used last year's figures, and the client lost trust in the report" is information. Only the second tells someone where to look.

image.label: Three steps: what happened, what it caused, what next
image.brief: 세 칸 인포그래픽. "What I saw" (눈 아이콘), "What it caused" (도미노 아이콘), "What next" (화살표 아이콘)가 왼쪽에서 오른쪽으로 연결.

cards.title: Labels start a defense. Details start a fix.
body: When feedback sounds like a judgment of who you are, your mind gets busy protecting that image. Energy goes to arguing, explaining or feeling bad, not to the work.
list: **"Not a team player"** → "You missed two handoff meetings this week"
**"Sloppy"** → "Three invoices went out without PO numbers"
**"Great job"** → "Calling the client before the deadline slipped saved the account"
cards.callout: Praise follows the same rule. Specific praise tells people what to repeat.

cards.title: Any work you can see, in any business.
body: A kitchen manager can say "the steak went out cold because it waited at the pass" instead of "you're slow." A warehouse lead can point to the mislabeled pallet instead of calling someone unreliable.
The same three steps work for a new hire or a ten-year veteran.
cards.softwareNote: Code reviews show this clearly. "This is messy" gets pushback. "This function does three jobs, which made the bug hard to find. Can we split it?" gets a fix.

cards.title: Specific isn't enough on its own.
body: Detailed notes on everything at once can bury the one point that matters. Pick the one or two changes with the biggest effect.
Timing and place matter too. Feedback given in front of others, or while someone is upset, can feel like an attack however well you word it.
And feedback only helps if the standard was clear in the first place. If nobody said what good looks like, start there.

cards.title: Now it's a cleaning company.
body: You run a home cleaning service. One cleaner keeps leaving streaks on bathroom mirrors and fixtures. A regular client complained for the second time.

options.text: Text them: "Another complaint. Please step it up."
options.feedback: It's quick, but it only says you're unhappy. They don't know which surfaces or what to change, so the streaks are likely to return.

options.text: Post a reminder about bathroom standards to the whole team
options.feedback: It avoids singling anyone out. But people rarely see themselves in a general reminder, and the client's problem stays with one person.

options.text: Meet at the next job, point to the streaks, show the dry-cloth finish, and ask for photos for a week
options.feedback: It costs you an hour, but the cleaner sees exactly what went wrong and how to fix it. The photos let you praise the fix, too.

cards.title: Describe the action, not the person.
body: Say what you saw, what it caused, and what to do next. That turns feedback from a judgment into something people can use.
**Try it today:** think of feedback you've been meaning to give. Write it in those three parts. Remove any word that describes the person.
